title: I open-sourced Kiln, a fast 3D asset prototyping toolchain for coding agents
author: MattMaxBuilds
selftext:
I've been working on AI-driven 3D generation for over a year now.

The problem I kept running into wasn't getting a model to produce some geometry. It was getting from a prompt to something I could inspect, revise, and actually bring into a game project without starting over every turn.

Diffusion-style 3D tools can give you a mesh, but often not much of a workflow around it. Letting an agent loosely script Blender or another full 3D package can also get chaotic once you need to make a precise change and keep everything else intact.

So I built Kiln.

Kiln is an open-source procedural 3D engine and agent toolchain for building editable assets in JavaScript.

For game development, I see its useful lane as fast, organized asset prototyping: props, machinery, vehicles, architecture, environments, set dressing, and rigid-body animation. An agent can build an asset, render it from several angles, inspect its structure, revise one part, and export a GLB without regenerating the whole thing.

It is also designed to be token efficient. The agent discovers primitives on demand instead of carrying the entire API in context, keeps source behind compact revision references, and makes targeted edits instead of resending or rewriting the whole program on every turn. I haven't turned that into a universal tokens-saved percentage because the actual cost depends on the model and harness, but reducing repeated context is part of the architecture.

Instead of returning a finished mesh in one shot, the agent works through the asset with Kiln's tools. In a typical run, the agent:

* discovers the available geometry and material helpers
* writes and validates the asset program
* renders multiple views and reads the structural measurements
* inspects individual parts, interiors, and animation states
* makes exact edits against an immutable source revision
* saves the JavaScript, GLB, preview, manifest, and revision history

The sandbox currently exposes 105 primitives and helpers across 12 categories. That includes core shapes, CSG booleans, curves, procedural materials, vehicle frames, wheel assemblies, architecture helpers, animation, inspection, and export tools. The point is to keep the agent from reinventing basic geometry math every time it needs a gear, tube, beveled box, dish, frame, or repeated assembly.

Kiln is also more than an MCP server. MCP is one adapter. The project includes the engine, CLI, Typescript Library, Agent Skills, and integrations for agent frameworks such as Strands. Bring any harness and multimodal model. The runtime, coding client, and GPU renderer can all run in different places, and the model mainly needs tool use and vision so it can inspect its own renders.

Most of the assets in the gallery section of the attached video are one-shot generations from simple prompts and took roughly a minute or so to generate. Some include revisions like the ones you see in the video. I didn't hand-polish them into production art. I wanted to show what the first pass can actually look like and how the same source can keep moving through the review and editing loop.

I also wouldn't suggest anyone to drop every generated GLB directly into a shipped game untouched. You still have your normal art direction, topology, materials, optimization, collision, LOD, rigging, and engine-integration standards. What Kiln is good at is getting to a concrete, editable prototype quickly and keeping the iteration organized after that.

Kiln is still in beta. Most of my integration testing so far has been in Three.js, including Kiln's own Three.js-based viewer, along with GLB validation tooling. The handoff has not been battle-tested nearly as much across real Unity, Godot, Unreal, and other engine pipelines. I am working toward a properly packaged 1.0 release, and feedback from real game projects will help me decide what needs to be tightened before then.

Rendering works locally, with an optional GPU renderer when compatible hardware is available. The project is MIT licensed.

GitHub: [https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln](https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln)

Interactive gallery and source: [https://kilnstudio.tools](https://kilnstudio.tools)

I'd be especially interested in feedback from game developers using Kiln in a real project. You could bring an asset into something you already have or build a small project around Kiln-generated assets. 

Please share what you made, what worked, what broke, and any fixes you had to make. Where is the most friction: pivots and scale, topology, materials, collision, LODs, hierarchy, animation, or something else?

replies.body:
sorry I'm new

eli5

can i take my current 2d game and ask astra to rebuild it in 3d with this?

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body:
Astra could probably figure out a lot of that, but I would not expect a clean one-click 2D to 3D migration. The workflow itself works with any model/harness that can make tool calls and inspect images.

The tricky part is not just generating 3D assets. You also have to decide camera style, how those assets fit into the game, and what happens to the existing mechanics and logic.

I would start by having it rebuild one scene or one asset in 3D and see how that goes before trying the whole game.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body: how do you handle textures?  Polygons are only part of the problem.  Without good textures, it'll always look like shit.

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body:
Textures are part of the pipeline too. It can generate procedural textures or use scanned PBR material sets. I have a bundled CC0 Poly Haven library for more irregular stuff like bark, soil, leather, etc., with albedo, normals, roughness, metalness, AO, emissive and so on.

Kiln spins up the GPU renderer for those so the agent can actually inspect the textured result and refine it, not just look at the geometry. I am also testing how this holds up across larger asset kits with shared materials, palettes, texture reuse, and keeping a set visually consistent.

It is still beta though, and there is definitely a lot of room to improve that side of it.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: That what I was going to ask, like, how good is it?  Sure, it can kinda make textures, and they work for prototyping, but not really for something you might want to ship.

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body:
Fair. The procedural textures are probably more prototype than ship right now. That is kind of the lane I am aiming at anyway.

The scanned PBR stuff can get you further, but I would still expect an artist to touch things up if you are trying to ship polished final art. I am mostly trying to get from placeholder assets to something useful in the game really fast.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: awesome, thank you for your work.  I will wait eagerly for your next post :)

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body:
Yeah, there are some really fast image-to-3D models now. Kiln is a bit of a different bet. I am betting that as coding models keep getting better, having the asset exist as something procedural and editable gives the agent more leverage over time than just getting a mesh back quickly.

The harder part is what happens after generation anyway - revising it, keeping a kit consistent, optimizing it, and making targeted changes without starting over.

comments.author: _xcud
comments.body: Tried Kiln in a Unity 6 sailing game (Built-in RP): a leeboard, a wind vane with a swivelling pennant, and a rolled bolt of sailcloth. The author → six-view review → targeted edit loop is excellent; each asset took 1–3 passes and renders were \~0.5 s on CPU. Friction was all in the handoff: (1) the prebuilt CLI failed on Node 18 with a module error rather than a version check; (2) GLB→FBX via Blender with bake-space-transform scrambled child-part offsets (our pennant landed 2.5 m away), so export with baking off; (3) single-sided `meshGeo` quads lost their back faces in Unity, so thin extrudes are safer; (4) `doubleSided` and anything beyond base colour don't survive; (5) a documented naming convention for animatable sub-parts would help engine-side scripts find pivots. Hierarchy and transforms were the biggest pain; scale, pivots and topology were fine.

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body: This is exactly the kind of feedback I was hoping people would kick back. Really useful - especially the Unity handoff stuff. I’m going to dig into these.

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body:
I took a proper pass at this and merged the first round of fixes here: [\#115](https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln/pull/115).

I added a Blender/Unity handoff guide, plus an experimental conversion path that uses Three.js’s `GLTFExporter` to turn Kiln scenes into GLBs. Kiln still uses its existing exporter by default while I keep qualifying the new path.

I also added actual import checks around hierarchy, pivots, materials, backfaces, animation, skin/morph deformation, and a Unity player build.

I was able to reproduce the Blender FBX issue with bake-space-transform on, so I documented the baking-off route. I also added guidance around named moving parts, direct GLB import, Unity root behavior, and checking clips in-engine rather than assuming a valid GLB means everything survived.

Your sailing-game test gave me a much better target than generic GLB validation. Thanks again for taking the time to write it up.

comments.author: kantorcodes1
comments.body: one thing I noticed in `src/cli.ts`: `render --out` goes through `prepareDestination()` straight into `writeFile()`, while `prepareDestination()` only creates the parent dir. if that write dies halfway, an existing GLB at `--out` can be lost. any reason not to write a sibling temp file and rename it after success? agents will probably reuse the same output path a lot.

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body: Good catch, thanks for flagging this. Fixed and merged using the sibling temp file + rename approach you suggested. Added tests confirming failed writes preserve the existing output, and verified repeated CLI exports with a GPU render. Credited you in the PR too: [https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln/pull/114](https://github.com/matthew-kissinger/kiln/pull/114)

replies.author: kantorcodes1
replies.body: nice, that's exactly the failure mode i was worried about. i work on HOL, where we maintain HOL Guard, an open-source local checkpoint before agent-run commands execute. Kiln looks like a clean fit: review `render --out`, `save`, and `source --out` before they write or replace files, so an agent can't silently clobber an asset. open to a small Guard-side extension?

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body: Yeah, definitely open to that. Happy to collaborate if anything on the Kiln side would make the integration cleaner too. Let me know what you have in mind.

replies.author: kantorcodes1
replies.body:
yep. smallest slice is `command.kiln`: start `src/codex_plugin_scanner/guard/runtime/command_kiln_extensions.py` and mirror `command_repo2nb_extensions.py`. review `render`, `generate`, `save`, and `import`; keep `assets`, plain `collections`, `asset` without `--restore`, and `view` automatic. add focused cases in `tests/test_guard_command_kiln_extensions.py`.

open a genuine draft PR directly to `hashgraph-online/hol-guard:main`: https://github.com/hashgraph-online/hol-guard/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

replies.author: MattMaxBuilds
replies.body: I can take a pass at this tomorrow and get a draft PR up. Thanks for scoping it out.

comments.author: MattMaxBuilds

A few people asked about characters, so I took that as an excuse to build a Jaeger.

Threw together a quick prototype tonight with Kiln and dropped it into a playable demo. 79 meters tall, fully articulated, walking, flying, blade combat, shoulder cannons, etc.

https://reddit.com/link/p9x4in3/video/me1hfeuganph1/player

All of the 3D assets in the prototype were made with Kiln too - the Jaeger, environment, cradle, targets, rails, the lot.

Still rough and I have barely tested yet, but it should give a better idea of where I am taking this.
